items.prompt: A metrics service stores 80 TB and ingests 300 000 writes/s; one database node handles about 20 000 writes/s.
items.why: Both write throughput and data size exceed one node → split the data. Replicas would each still take all 300k writes.

items.prompt: A blog platform's database is fine on writes, but reads have grown 10× and the primary's CPU is saturated by varied queries.
items.why: The problem is read-only load of varied queries → add read replicas. Writes and size are fine, so sharding isn't needed yet.

items.prompt: Orders are partitioned by created_at ranges per month; every write goes to the newest partition and that node is overloaded.
items.why: A hot last shard from a monotonically increasing range key is a shard-key problem → hash the key or use a compound key.

items.prompt: Your cache tier uses hash % N across nodes, and adding one node empties most of the cache.
items.why: The split already exists. The problem is placement remapping when N changes → consistent hashing (or fixed slots).

items.prompt: A chat app stores billions of messages, and almost every query is 'latest messages of conversation X'.
items.why: Huge data with a natural partition key that every hot query includes → shard by conversation_id.

items.prompt: At 9am a flood of signup writes spikes for 2 minutes, then the database is idle again; average load is low.
items.why: A short burst over a low average → buffer it with a queue. Sharding is for sustained load beyond one node.

items.prompt: In a multi-tenant SaaS sharded by tenant_id, one enterprise customer generates 40% of all traffic and overloads its shard; they pay for that volume, so throttling them is not an option.
items.why: A hot partition from a skewed key, and limiting is ruled out → split that tenant further (salted sub-keys or a dedicated shard). That's a partitioning fix.
